children: By Staff Writer

The East African Community has reached a landmark agreement on 95 per cent of its revised Rules of Origin, marking a significant milestone on the path to a fully integrated, duty-free single market. However, progress has stalled over the remaining five per cent, with partner states divided on how to classify goods from sensitive sectors, including spices, textiles, motor vehicles and hides and skins.
The agreement on the harmonisation of the revised Rules of Origin marks a significant step towards achieving a fully integrated, duty-free single market within the eight-nation economic bloc.

The EAC Rules of Origin are a set of criteria used to distinguish between goods produced within the EAC Customs Territory, which are eligible for the community’s preferential tariff treatment, and goods produced outside the territory, which attract import duties specified in the Common External Tariff (CET).

The agreement allows for the harmonisation of trading standards for thousands of goods traded within the region, representing a significant achievement in the implementation of the EAC Customs Union, the first pillar of regional integration.

But according to the Sectoral Council on Trade, Industry, Finance and Investments (SCTIFI), a stubborn five per cent deadlock is holding up the final deal, with partner states locked in a fierce debate over how to define the origins of goods from critical sectors, specifically spices, automobiles, textiles (yarn and threads of cotton), apparel and clothing accessories, and hides and skins.
The region says there has been substantial progress in the comprehensive review of the EAC Rules of Origin.

These rules refer to the specific tests and guidelines used to distinguish between goods produced within the EAC Customs Territory that are eligible for preferential tax treatment and goods produced outside the regional bloc.

The Council notes that further evidence-based analysis is required with regard to regional production capacity, the availability and competitiveness of inputs, industrial demand, trade flows, import dependency, investment potential, employment creation and opportunities for value addition.“Significant progress has been made in the comprehensive review of the EAC Rules of Origin (RoO), which covers both the general provisions and the product-specific list rules. However, a number of issues remain to be considered, including product-specific rules for selected tariff lines,” says the Council.“The Sectoral Council on Trade, Industry, Finance and Investment took note of the progress made in the review of the EAC Rules of Origin, with 100 per cent of the general provisions and over 95 per cent of the product-specific rules having been agreed upon. The currently applicable rules of origin were maintained for the products for which consensus could not be reached.”The Council said an assessment of key factors, including the potential impact of alternative rules of origin on industrialisation, regional value chains, competitiveness, trade facilitation and alignment with EAC priorities and comparable regional trade arrangements, would facilitate informed decision-making and consensus among partner states on the outstanding products.“In view of the limited number of outstanding product lines and the divergent positions maintained by partner states, the meeting observed that the unresolved matters require further evidence-based analysis with regard to regional production capacity, the availability and competitiveness of inputs, industrial demand, trade flows, import dependency, investment potential, employment creation and value addition opportunities,” the Council said of the decisions made at its latest meeting, held in Arusha from May 29 May to June 4.
The Council agreed to adopt the revised EAC Rules of Origin, incorporating all the agreed amendments to the Protocol on the Establishment of the EAC Customs Union.
They then referred the revised rules to the Sectoral Council on Legal and Judicial Affairs (SCLJA) for legal review.
The Council maintained the currently applicable rules of origin for outstanding products, pending the outcome of targeted studies and further consideration by the relevant EAC bodies.

The Council directed the EAC Secretariat and partner states to conduct targeted sectoral analyses of the outstanding products, to establish an objective basis for determining the most appropriate product-specific rules of origin.

To qualify as originating in the EAC, goods must either be wholly produced in the EAC or undergo sufficient work or processing in the EAC using materials imported from third countries under the region’s duty remission scheme.
Materials imported from third countries are regarded as non-originating materials.

According to the Protocol on the Establishment of the EAC Customs Union, goods whose inputs have benefitted from duty waivers must be sold outside the EAC. If such goods are sold in the EAC Customs Territory, duties, levies and other charges as set out in the CET must be paid.
It also stipulates that the sale of such goods in the territory should be limited to 20 per cent of a company’s annual production, and that they should be subject to duty as set out in the CET.

Under the region’s four-band CET, imports of finished products from countries outside the bloc attract a 35 percent duty; 25 percent for intermediate products available in the EAC region; 10 percent for intermediate products not available in the EAC region; and 0 percent for raw materials and capital goods.

The Council, in a meeting held in Arusha in November 2024, recommended a complete review of these rules rather than piecemeal changes on various contentious products, such as refined sugar for industrial use.

The proposed review of the EAC Rules of Origin 2015 followed concerns by the business community that existing rules, which have not been reviewed in more than a decade, have failed to respond to the changing business environment brought about by new free trade areas such as the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) and the Tripartite Free Trade Area (TFTA).

In 2016, the Council directed that the review of the RoO 2015 be undertaken after the completion of the comprehensive review of the Common External Tariff (CET). The revised four band CET took effect on 1 July 2022.

In August 2024, Kenya wrote to the EAC Secretariat proposing initiation of the comprehensive review of the EAC Rules of Origin 2015, with a further proposal on the importation of raw sugar to manufacture sugar for industrial use.
